# `mine_rehabilitation`

*Revegetation of a mine or quarry site against an undisturbed reference over several same-season dates*

**Topic:** Energy and mining · **Status:** Runs out of the box · **Tags:** `mining`, `rehabilitation`, `closure`, `revegetation`, `ndvi`, `time-series`

## The question it answers

> Is the disturbed ground of this site returning to vegetation, how far has it got, and where is it stuck or going backwards?

A mine is closed when the ground it disturbed has been returned to a stable, self-sustaining cover, and the question every
operator, regulator and neighbouring community asks is "how much of it is back, and is it still improving?". Walking the
site answers that for the plots you visit; satellites answer it for every hectare, every year, with the same method.
This pipeline compares the site's greenness with an undisturbed reference on each date (which divides out rainy and dry
seasons), follows that ratio through the years, and sorts every pixel into recovered, recovering, stalled, bare or
declining, with pit lakes and tailings ponds kept apart so that water is never reported as bare ground.

## When to use it

- You manage, regulate or monitor a mine, quarry, tailings facility or spoil dump and need to know where revegetation is working and where it is not.
- You want to show progress toward a closure objective as a repeatable annual number, or find the patches that need attention (erosion, poor topsoil, compaction) before a field visit.
- You monitor land after informal (galamsey) mining and want to know whether it is recovering by itself.

**Do not use it for:**

- A compliance finding. Completion criteria are set by regulators and are normally field-based (cover, species, soil, stability); greenness is evidence, not proof.
- Judging the *kind* of vegetation. A dense weed or a plantation is as green as the forest it replaced. Use field plots, or a trained [`land_cover`](land_cover.md) check, for composition.
- Mapping the footprint of a mine or the loss of forest to it. Use [`forest_change`](forest_change.md) or [`landcover_change`](landcover_change.md) for that, then give the result here as the `site`.
- Predicting when a site will meet its criteria. The trend of a few dates is not a forecast and the pipeline offers none.

## How it works

Is the disturbed ground of a mine, tailings facility or quarry coming back, and where is it not?

Greenness (NDVI) of the site is compared, on every date, with an undisturbed **reference** observed on the same
date, which takes the season out: ``RRI = site NDVI / median reference NDVI``. RRI of 1 means the site is as
green as the reference; 0.8 (``recovered_rri``) is read as recovered. Give ``dates`` (three or more,
``YYYY-MM`` or ``YYYY-MM-DD``, in the **same season** of different years) and at least one of ``site`` and
``reference`` (polygon files, any coordinate system):

* ``site`` only: the reference is chosen automatically as persistently vegetated land (median NDVI >=
  ``reference_min_ndvi``) outside the site and its ``reference_buffer_m`` margin.
* ``reference`` only: everything outside the reference is assessed.
* both: the site is assessed against your reference polygons (any part inside the site is ignored).

Each assessed pixel gets the mean RRI of the last ``recent_dates`` dates and the least-squares trend of RRI
over all dates, and is classed: recovered (RRI >= ``recovered_rri``); recovering (trend >= +``trend_threshold``
per year); declining (<= -``trend_threshold``); bare or sparse (RRI < ``bare_rri``); otherwise stalled. Pixels that were
water on at least half their observations (MNDWI > ``mndwi_threshold``) are a separate class, not "bare". Cloud is
nodata, never a class, and a pixel needs ``min_observations`` clear dates. Dates seen on less than
``min_valid_fraction`` of the site, or with fewer than ``min_reference_px`` reference pixels, are listed and
left out.

Written: ``rehab_status.tif`` (classes), ``recovery_index.tif`` (recent RRI), ``recovery_trend.tif`` (RRI per
year), ``reference_mask.tif`` and ``rehabilitation_timeseries.csv`` (site median RRI per date).

Limits. Greenness is not ecosystem recovery: a dense weed or plantation monoculture is "recovered" by this
measure and a dry-season woodland reference makes the ratio unstable. The reference must be the ecosystem the closure
plan is aiming for. Per-pixel trends come from a handful of noisy dates; read the site-level series
(``site_trend_per_year``) before the per-pixel trend map, and sieve the class raster before counting patches.
The pipeline does not predict when a site will meet its closure criteria, and it is not a compliance finding:
completion criteria are set by regulators and are normally field-based.

**Method, step by step**

1. NDVI and MNDWI are computed on each date from cloud-masked Sentinel-2 / Landsat scenes, all aligned to the grid of the first.
2. The relative recovery index (RRI) of a pixel is its NDVI divided by the median NDVI of the reference pixels on the same date, which divides out the season.
3. Each pixel gets the mean RRI of the most recent dates and the least-squares trend of its RRI against time, and is classed recovered, recovering, declining, bare or stalled by the thresholds shown with the run. Pixels that were water on at least half of their observations are a separate class.
4. Cloud is nodata. A pixel needs the minimum number of clear dates, and a date seen on too little of the site, or with too few reference pixels, is listed and left out.

**Inputs and accounts**

Sentinel-2 L2A from the open catalogues; no account is needed. You supply the **site** (polygons of the disturbed or
rehabilitated ground) and, ideally, a **reference** (polygons of the undisturbed ecosystem the closure plan aims for) as
GeoJSON, shapefile or GeoPackage files in any coordinate system. If you give only the site, the reference is chosen
automatically as persistently green land outside the site and a margin around it; the run says so in `reference_source`.

## Run it

```bash
pygeovision channel mine_rehabilitation \
    --bbox -2.20 6.00 -2.05 6.12 \
    --dates 2020-02,2021-02,2022-02,2023-02,2024-02 \
    --param site=./tailings_dump_3.geojson \
    --param reference=./intact_forest.geojson \
    --output ./dump3_rehabilitation
```

```python
from pygeovision import PyGeoVision

client = PyGeoVision()
bbox = (-2.20, 6.00, -2.05, 6.12)  # min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat
result = client.pipeline(
    "mine_rehabilitation",
    bbox=bbox,
    dates=["2020-02", "2021-02", "2022-02", "2023-02", "2024-02"],
    site="./tailings_dump_3.geojson",
    reference="./intact_forest.geojson",
    output_dir="./dump3_rehabilitation",
)
if not result.success:
    raise SystemExit(result.error)
print(result.stats)
```

### Arguments

Every pipeline also takes `--bbox` and `--output`; see [common options](../index.md#common-options). `providers=[...]` (CLI `--provider`) restricts the data providers where the pipeline downloads imagery.

| Argument | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dates` | `None` | Five or so dates, **one per year in the same month**, as `YYYY-MM` or `YYYY-MM-DD`. At least three are needed. **Required.** |
| `site` | `None` | Polygon file of the disturbed or rehabilitated ground to assess. Give `site`, `reference` or both. |
| `reference` | `None` | Polygon file of undisturbed land to compare with. Any part inside the site is ignored (and counted in `reference_overlap_removed_px`). |
| `recovered_rri` | `0.8` | A pixel whose recent RRI reaches this is *recovered* (default 0.8). It is a working threshold, not a regulatory criterion. |
| `bare_rri` | `0.4` | Below this recent RRI a pixel with no clear trend is *bare or sparse* (default 0.4). |
| `trend_threshold` | `0.03` | Change in RRI per year that counts as *recovering* (up) or *declining* (down) (default 0.03, so 0.12 over four years). |
| `recent_dates` | `2` | How many of the latest dates are averaged for the current level (default 2). |
| `min_observations` | `3` | Clear dates a pixel needs to be classed (default 3; cannot be lower, two dates cannot show a trend). |
| `min_valid_fraction` | `0.6` | A date seen on less than this share of the site is left out (default 0.6). |
| `min_reference_px` | `30` | Fewest reference pixels a date needs to be trusted, and the fewest the run needs overall (default 30). |
| `reference_min_ndvi` | `0.5` | Automatic reference only: lowest median NDVI for land to count as reference (default 0.5). Lower it for savanna or dry woodland. |
| `reference_buffer_m` | `100.0` | Automatic reference only: margin kept clear around the site, in metres (default 100). |
| `mndwi_threshold` | `0.0` | MNDWI above this marks water; a pixel that is water on half or more of its dates is the *water* class (default 0). |
| `cloud_cover_max` | `30.0` | Scene cloud limit in per cent (default 30). |

### Choosing dates and inputs

Use the **same month in every year**, in the season when the reference is green and the sky is clearest (for a tropical
site, the dry season). Different seasons are not comparable even after the reference ratio; the run warns when the dates
are more than 75 days apart within the year (`season_warning`). Five or more years give a trend worth looking at; three
is the minimum. A bare year is refused because it cannot place a date in a season.

## Modify it

Three levels, from least to most effort. Start at the first; most changes need nothing more.

### 1. Change a setting

Every argument in the table above is changed per run, with `--param NAME=VALUE` on the command line or `NAME=VALUE` in Python. The changes people make most with this pipeline:

- **Your site and reference.** `site` and `reference` are polygon files; give one or both. Without a reference, an automatic reference is chosen from land with median NDVI above `reference_min_ndvi` (lower it for savanna or dry woodland).
- **Class thresholds.** `recovered_rri` (default 0.8), `bare_rri` (0.4) and `trend_threshold` (0.03 per year) are working thresholds, not regulatory criteria. Change them and record your values.
- **How much data per pixel.** `min_observations` (at least 3), `recent_dates` and `min_valid_fraction` control which dates and pixels count.

After any change, read the **parameters** block of `run_summary.json`: it records the values that were used, so a result can always be traced to its settings.

### 2. Change where the data comes from, and what is written

- **Providers.** `providers=["planetary_computer"]` (CLI `--provider planetary_computer`) restricts the catalogues the pipeline searches; see [Providers](../../data/providers.md).
- **Output.** `output_dir` (CLI `--output`) is the folder for the rasters, `run_summary.json` and `deliverables/`. Rebuild maps and reports from a finished run without re-downloading: [Rebuilding](../../reporting/rebuilding.md).
- **Your own area.** A bounding box, or the true shape of an administrative area ([boundaries](../../data/boundaries.md)).

### 3. Change the method (write a variant)

The pipeline is the class `MineRehabilitationPipeline` in `pygeovision/ai/pipelines/timeseries.py`. To change its behaviour without editing the package, subclass it, give the subclass a new `name`, and override `run`. This changes the defaults of one run; the original is untouched:

```python
from pygeovision import PyGeoVision
from pygeovision.ai.pipelines import pipeline_catalogue

Base = pipeline_catalogue()["mine_rehabilitation"]


class MyMineRehabilitation(Base):
    name = "my_mine_rehabilitation"          # a new name, so files and reports do not clash with the original

    def run(self, bbox, output_dir, **kwargs):
        kwargs.setdefault("recovered_rri", 1.2)        # your default (the built-in one is 0.8)
        return super().run(bbox, output_dir, **kwargs)

client = PyGeoVision()
result = MyMineRehabilitation(client).run(bbox, "./variant")   # plus the same date arguments as in Run it
```

Calling `.run` on your class does not need any registration. To use it by name in `client.pipeline(...)`, register it in the process; to write a pipeline from scratch see [Write your own pipeline](../custom.md). The built-in `pygeovision channel` command runs only the built-in pipelines.

To change the numbers of the method itself (a threshold written in the code, not exposed as an argument), read `MineRehabilitationPipeline.run` in `pygeovision/ai/pipelines/timeseries.py`; the *How it works* section above lists the steps in the order the code takes them. Whatever you change, compare the new run with the old one ([comparing runs](../results.md#comparing-runs)) and validate the result against reference data before you use it ([validation](../../data/validation.md)).

## What you get

| File | Layer | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `rehab_status.tif` | Rehabilitation status | classes |
| `recovery_index.tif` | Recent relative recovery index (1 = as green as the reference) | continuous values |
| `recovery_trend.tif` | Change in RRI per year | continuous values |
| `reference_mask.tif` | Reference pixels used | classes |

Written next to these: `run_summary.json` (every figure and parameter) and, unless switched off, a `deliverables/` folder with maps, GeoPackage/GeoJSON vectors and PDF, Word and Excel reports ([Deliverables](../../reporting/index.md)). **255 in a class raster and NaN in a continuous raster mean no data**, never a class ([Core concepts](../../getting-started/concepts.md)).

**Classes in the example run**

| Raster | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `rehab_status.tif` | 0 | Outside the assessed area (or reference) |
| `rehab_status.tif` | 1 | Recovered (at or above the recovered level) |
| `rehab_status.tif` | 3 | Stalled (partial, not rising) |
| `rehab_status.tif` | 4 | Bare or sparse |
| `rehab_status.tif` | 5 | Declining (falling) |
| `rehab_status.tif` | 6 | Water (pit lake, pond) |
| `reference_mask.tif` | 0 | Not reference |
| `reference_mask.tif` | 1 | Reference |

## Reading the results

**Start with the site-level series**, `rehabilitation_timeseries.csv` and `site_trend_per_year`. A median RRI that climbs from
0.2 to 0.6 over five years is a site that is recovering; one that sits at 0.5 for three years has stalled. Then look at
`rehab_status.tif`: green is recovered, light green recovering, yellow stalled, brown bare, red declining, blue water.

The **reference sets the meaning of every number.** RRI of 0.8 means "four-fifths as green as the ecosystem you chose". If
the reference is a closed forest, a good grassland cover will never reach it; if it is open savanna, a young plantation
will pass it early. Check `reference_mask.tif` and say in any report which reference was used.

Per-pixel classes rest on five or so noisy dates, so edges flicker. Sieve before counting patches
(`pygeovision postprocess sieve`), and treat a single declining pixel as noise and a declining *patch* as a finding.

**Notes from the report**

- RRI of 1 means as green as the reference on the same date; the recovered level is a threshold you set (0.8 by default), not a regulatory criterion.
- Read the site-level series (table and chart) before the per-pixel trend map: the series averages thousands of pixels, while a pixel's trend rests on a handful of noisy dates.
- A class raster this fine is speckled; sieve it before counting patches or reporting hectares by parcel.

## Next steps with the output

1. Open `rehabilitation_timeseries.csv` and plot `site_rri_median` against date; look at the `note` column for dates that were left out.
2. Open `rehab_status.tif` over the imagery in QGIS and walk the red (declining) and brown (bare) patches in the field: erosion gullies, compaction, acid or saline spoil and failed topsoil placement are the usual causes, and the satellite cannot tell which.
3. Sieve and count by domain or by closure parcel:

   ```bash
   pygeovision postprocess sieve ./dump3_rehabilitation/rehab_status.tif --min-pixels 8 \
       --output ./dump3_rehabilitation/rehab_status_sieved.tif
   pygeovision postprocess class-stats ./dump3_rehabilitation/rehab_status_sieved.tif
   ```
4. Run it again next year with one more date; the series is the record.

## Limitations

- Greenness is not ecosystem recovery. A weed cover or a monoculture counts as recovered; a woodland reference that is leafless in the dry season makes the ratio unstable.
- The result is only as good as the reference. It should be the ecosystem the closure plan aims for; an automatic reference is just persistently green land outside the site.
- Dates from different seasons are not comparable even after the reference ratio; use the same month in each year.
- The pipeline does not say when a site will meet its closure criteria and is not a compliance finding. Completion criteria are set by regulators and are normally field-based.
- Dust, wet soil and shadow on tailings and spoil can change NDVI independently of vegetation.

## What to do when…

| Symptom | What to do |
|---|---|
| "Give `site` ... or `reference`" | The pipeline cannot tell which ground is being rehabilitated. Pass `--param site=file.geojson` and/or `--param reference=file.geojson`. |
| "Only N reference pixels were found" | The automatic reference found too little green land. Widen the bbox to take in undisturbed vegetation, lower `reference_min_ndvi`, or draw `reference` polygons. |
| "do not overlap the imagery" | The polygon file is outside the bbox or in the wrong coordinate system (a file without a coordinate system is refused). Check it in QGIS. |
| A date is listed under `dates_left_out` | The site was under cloud, the reference was too dry (NDVI below 0.1), or too few reference pixels were seen. Choose another scene for that year or accept the gap; three usable dates are enough to run. |
| Everything is "bare" or "stalled" | The reference may be much greener than anything a young site can reach (a closed forest). Check `reference_mask.tif`, and compare with a reference that matches the closure target. |
| Large area of "declining" on a site you know is fine | Dates in different seasons or a dry year. Check `season_warning` and `reference_ndvi_median` in the CSV; the ratio is unstable when the reference is dormant. |
| Pit lakes or tailings ponds show as bare | They should be the water class. A shallow, turbid pond may fall under the threshold; lower `mndwi_threshold` (for example to -0.1) and look again. |
| `success=False` with "No usable imagery" | Widen the date window; see the [troubleshooting guide](../../getting-started/troubleshooting.md). |
| Warning about an unknown argument | A misspelt `--param`: the message suggests the closest valid name. |
